rubric.why: Heat is distinguished by its nature as energy transferred between bodies because of a temperature difference.
rubric.description: Defines heat as energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
rubric.how: Award for stating that heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body.

rubric.why: Temperature describes how hot or cold a body is.
rubric.description: Defines temperature as the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
rubric.how: Award for identifying temperature as a measure of hotness or coldness.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

items.followUp: State the law of conservation of momentum and explain it using two colliding carts.

rubric.why: The law states that total momentum does not change in an isolated system.
rubric.description: States the law of conservation of momentum.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.

rubric.why: The equation expresses equality of total momentum before and after an interaction.
rubric.description: Gives the momentum-conservation equation.
rubric.how: Award for a correct equation or equivalent statement that total momentum before equals total momentum after.

rubric.why: The example must describe an interaction between balls.
rubric.description: Identifies the balls collision example.
rubric.how: Award for describing two balls colliding.

rubric.why: The example illustrates that momentum transferred between the balls does not change their combined momentum.
rubric.description: Explains how the collision demonstrates conservation.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the momentum lost by one ball is gained by the other, so their total momentum remains unchanged.

modelAnswer: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on it.
Thus, total momentum before interaction = total momentum after interaction.
For two balls of masses m₁ and m₂, with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂:
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
When two balls collide, one ball may lose momentum while the other gains it; the total momentum of both balls remains unchanged.

items.followUp: A bus slows uniformly from 25 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 3 s. Find its retardation.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the initial velocity, final velocity and time in SI units.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award for identifying u = 30 m s⁻¹, v = 15 m s⁻¹ and t = 5 s.

rubric.why: This is the relation between velocity change, time and acceleration.
rubric.description: Selects the acceleration formula.
rubric.how: Award for writing a = (v − u)/t or an equivalent formula.

rubric.why: The values are substituted in the correct order with units.
rubric.description: Substitutes the given values correctly.
rubric.how: Award for substituting v = 15 m s⁻¹, u = 30 m s⁻¹ and t = 5 s.

rubric.why: The negative sign shows the acceleration is opposite to the direction of motion.
rubric.description: Finds the acceleration.
rubric.how: Award for obtaining −3 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Retardation is the magnitude of the negative acceleration.
rubric.description: States the retardation with its unit.
rubric.how: Award for giving retardation as 3 m s⁻².

modelAnswer: Given: u = 30 m s⁻¹, v = 15 m s⁻¹, t = 5 s.
Formula: a = (v − u)/t.
Substitution: a = (15 m s⁻¹ − 30 m s⁻¹)/(5 s).
a = −3 m s⁻².
Retardation = magnitude of a = 3 m s⁻².

items.followUp: Explain how petroleum is formed and name two fossil fuels other than petroleum.

rubric.why: Fossil fuels originate from ancient organic remains transformed over a long period.
rubric.description: Explains the formation of fossil fuels.
rubric.how: Award for stating that fossil fuels form from buried plant or animal remains over millions of years, usually under heat and pressure.

rubric.why: These are examples of fossil fuels.
rubric.description: Gives examples of fossil fuels.
rubric.how: Award for naming two examples such as coal, petroleum or natural gas.

rubric.why: Uranium and thorium are examples of nuclear fuels.
rubric.description: Identifies nuclear fuels and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for naming uranium or thorium as a nuclear fuel.

rubric.why: Nuclear fuels release energy through reactions in atomic nuclei.
rubric.description: Explains how nuclear fuels release energy.
rubric.how: Award for stating that nuclear fuels release energy through nuclear reactions, such as fission.

modelAnswer: Fossil fuels are formed from the buried remains of plants and animals over millions of years under heat and pressure.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels.
Nuclear fuels are substances, such as uranium and thorium, whose atomic nuclei can release energy in nuclear reactions.
In a nuclear power station, energy is commonly released by fission of the fuel's nuclei.

items.followUp: A steering wheel has a radius of 20 cm. Find the torque produced by a couple of 40 N.

rubric.why: The force and radius must be identified, with the radius converted to metres.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award for identifying F = 50 N and r = 0.16 m.

rubric.why: For forces applied at opposite sides of the steering wheel, the perpendicular distance between their lines of action is the diameter.
rubric.description: Finds the arm of the couple.
rubric.how: Award for finding the couple arm as 2r = 0.32 m.

rubric.why: Torque of a couple equals either force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces.
rubric.description: Writes the torque formula.
rubric.how: Award for using torque = force × couple arm.

rubric.why: The force is multiplied by the calculated arm of the couple.
rubric.description: Substitutes values into the formula.
rubric.how: Award for substituting 50 N and 0.32 m.

rubric.why: The product gives the torque, expressed in newton metres.
rubric.description: Gives the final torque with unit.
rubric.how: Award for obtaining 16 N m.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 50 N, r = 16 cm = 0.16 m.
The couple arm is the diameter of the steering wheel: d = 2r = 2 × 0.16 m = 0.32 m.
Formula: torque of a couple = Fd.
Substitution: torque = 50 N × 0.32 m.
Torque = 16 N m.

items.followUp: A square plate has a side of 5 mm. Find the pressure on it when a force of 10 N acts normally on it.

rubric.why: The force and side length are correctly identified, and the length is converted to SI units.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award for identifying F = 20 N and side = 10 mm = 0.01 m.

rubric.why: The area of a square is its side multiplied by itself.
rubric.description: Finds the area of the nail head.
rubric.how: Award for obtaining an area of 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².

rubric.why: Pressure is force per unit area.
rubric.description: Writes the pressure formula.
rubric.how: Award for using P = F/A.

rubric.why: The force and area are substituted correctly.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values with units.
rubric.how: Award for substituting 20 N and 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².

rubric.why: Dividing force by area gives pressure in pascals.
rubric.description: Gives the final pressure with unit.
rubric.how: Award for obtaining 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 20 N, side = 10 mm = 0.01 m.
Area of the square head: A = side² = (0.01 m)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Formula: P = F/A.
Substitution: P = 20 N/(1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
Pressure = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

rubric.why: Nuclear physics studies the nucleus of the atom and its properties.
rubric.description: Defines nuclear physics.
rubric.how: Award for stating that nuclear physics is the study of atomic nuclei, including their structure or properties.

Nuclear physics is the branch of physics that studies the structure and properties of atomic nuclei.

items.followUp: Give two reasons why scientists use standard units of measurement.

rubric.why: SI provides a common system of measurement that scientists can use internationally.
rubric.description: Explains that SI units provide a universal standard.

rubric.why: A shared system helps scientists compare, communicate and reproduce measurements without confusion.
rubric.description: Explains how standard units help scientific work.
rubric.how: Award for giving a valid benefit, such as easier communication, comparison or avoidance of confusion.

modelAnswer: S.I. units provide a common standard of measurement used by scientists throughout the world.
They make measurements and results easier to communicate and compare, and help avoid confusion.
